summary:
IMMOONITY is a web app and API that estimates an astronaut's risk of immune problems before and during a mission and explains the result in plain language.

Spaceflight weakens immune control: in a study of 22 ISS crew members, 17 reactivated a latent herpesvirus during six-month missions, and viral shedding becomes more common on longer flights. Crews going to the Moon and Mars will need an earlier warning, far from Earth.

We built two models. The pre-flight model turns fitness tests (VO2max, push-ups, pull-ups) into a risk of latent virus reactivation; it is a Bayesian logistic regression fitted to those 22 crew members. The in-flight model combines lab markers measured in NASA ISS studies (IL-6, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, cortisol and EBV DNA in saliva) with mission length to estimate the risk of multi-system immune dysregulation. Every result comes with a 90% interval, the factors behind it, what-if scenarios and sources. We checked marker variability and thresholds on NASA OSDR data from the Inspiration4 crew.

IMMOONITY turns a few measurements into an early, explainable signal for crews and flight surgeons. It is a research demonstrator, not a medical device.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
IMMOONITY estimates immune risk for astronauts at two points and explains the result.
• Pre-flight model (during training): sex, VO2max, push-ups and pull-ups → risk of latent herpesvirus reactivation (EBV, VZV, CMV) during a ~6-month mission.
• In-flight model (during the mission): IL-6, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) and cortisol (baseline and in flight), EBV DNA in saliva and mission length → risk that at least 2 of 4 immune subsystems (inflammation, leukocyte shift, EBV reactivation, stress axis) are involved by the end of the mission.
• Consultant: every result comes with a 90% interval and a level, the markers that drive it, what-if scenarios (for example, "if cortisol normalises, the risk drops from 45% to 11%"), recommendations, limitations and sources, in English or Russian. The rule-based consultant can also build a prompt that keeps a large language model grounded in these facts.
• Web demo: https://immoonity.onrender.com; REST API: /predict, /api/models.

HOW IT WORKS
• Pre-flight model: Bayesian logistic regression fitted to 22 ISS crew members (Agha et al., 2020). The fitness index weights VO2max, push-ups and pull-ups 0.4 / 0.3 / 0.3, following the published risk reductions (−29% for aerobic fitness, −39% for upper-body endurance). Leave-one-out AUC 0.65, Brier score 0.18: the sample is small, so the app shows wide intervals rather than false precision.
• In-flight model: a subsystem counts as involved above an absolute limit (IL-6 > 7 pg/mL, NLR > 3.5, cortisol > 550 nmol/L, salivary EBV DNA > 129 copies/mL) or when the rise from the person's own baseline exceeds the reference change value from biological variation (IL-6 +71%, NLR +46%, cortisol +39%). Thresholds are soft, so the risk changes smoothly. Mission length adds +0.21 log-odds per doubling, derived from herpesvirus shedding on short flights vs ISS missions (Rooney et al., 2019). Beyond 437 days, the longest human spaceflight so far, the app warns, widens the interval and estimates the cumulative radiation dose against NASA's 600 mSv career limit.
• NASA data: we checked the model on NASA OSDR data from the Inspiration4 crew. Within-person variability: NLR 20.8% (the model assumes 19.8%, OSD-569), IL-6 27% (the model assumes 30%, OSD-575). One day after landing the IL-6 rise threshold was crossed in 2 of 4 crew members and the NLR threshold in none. A baseline taken 3 days before launch changed the decision for one person, so the app asks for baselines 1–2 months before launch.
• Data integrity: in our original group-level dataset the outcome was the sum of the inputs in 37 of 41 rows (target leakage). We do not fit the in-flight model to it; its parameters come from published studies, and we removed an earlier AUC 0.98 claim.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT
• An early, explainable signal for crews and flight surgeons from a few lab markers measured in NASA ISS studies.
• Fitness targets for crew training tied to reactivation risk.
• Mission planning: shows how immune risk grows from ISS missions to Moon and Mars mission lengths.
• Open and auditable: every parameter traces to a publication or a NASA dataset (MODEL.md in the repository).

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES
Python (Flask, NumPy, Matplotlib, pytest), HTML/CSS/JavaScript (GSAP), Gunicorn, Docker, GitHub Actions, Render cloud hosting, NASA OSDR API.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE
• One consultant for both pre-flight fitness and in-flight biomarkers.
• Change is judged against each astronaut's own baseline, not only population cut-offs.
• It shows its uncertainty: every risk has a 90% interval, and extrapolation beyond flown mission lengths is flagged.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED
• Small samples (22 ISS crew members; 4 Inspiration4 crew members) and no open individual-level outcome data. Next step: validation on NASA LSDA data (Integrated Immune study).
• Sampling time (cortisol varies over the day), sample type and age are not yet modelled.
• Safety: a research demonstrator, not a medical device; decisions stay with physicians.

USE OF SI
An AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic) was used to help write and review code (API, model training, tests, deployment), check the literature, translate and draft the documentation, this description and the demo deck. The project idea and the choice of markers come from the team.
dataRefs: NASA OSDR OSD-569: Inspiration4 complete blood count (NLR)
NASA OSDR OSD-575: Inspiration4 serum cytokines (IL-6)
NASA OSDR OSD-571: Inspiration4 plasma metabolomics (cortisol check)
NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) and API
projectRefs: Agha et al., 2020: fitness and viral reactivation in 22 ISS crew members (pre-flight model data)
Zeitlin et al., 2013: radiation dose in transit to Mars
Forget et al., 2017: normal NLR range
